faq.a: Excess glucose is reduced to sorbitol in nerves and lenses, causing osmotic stress and cellular damage, leading to neuropathy and cataracts.
It slows further progression but rarely reverses structural damage; early detection is key.
faq.q: Can tight glucose control reverse established complications?

faq.a: Assess vascular supply, perform a monofilament test, and start off‑loading plus empirical antibiotics while arranging wound care.
faq.q: What is the first step if a patient presents with a foot ulcer?

exam: A 55‑year‑old diabetic presents with new‑onset blurry vision – what bedside test would you perform and why? — Perform fundoscopy to look for microaneurysms or neovascularisation; early changes guide urgency of laser therapy.

Explain how you would stage diabetic nephropathy using only urine dipstick and blood pressure readings when ACR is unavailable. — Use dipstick protein (trace‑plus suggests microalbuminuria) and monitor for hypertension; escalating proteinuria and rising BP indicate progression.

A patient with HIV on antiretrovirals develops peripheral neuropathy – how does this affect your management of diabetic neuropathy? — Consider drug‑induced neuropathy, optimise glycaemic control, avoid metformin if renal function is impaired, and use gabapentin cautiously due to drug interactions.

You suspect proliferative retinopathy but have no laser equipment – what is your next step? — Refer urgently to a centre with laser or intravitreal anti‑VEGF capability; meanwhile control glucose and blood pressure tightly.

During a ward round you find a diabetic with a painless foot ulcer and a normal monofilament test – what does this suggest? — Possible vascular (ischemic) ulcer; obtain ankle‑brachial index and consider arterial imaging.

A diabetic patient presents with acute chest pain and an HbA1c of 9 % – what immediate investigations and management priorities apply? — ECG, cardiac enzymes, give aspirin, nitroglycerin, and start high‑intensity statin; also optimise glucose urgently.

How would you differentiate hypertensive retinopathy from diabetic retinopathy on exam? — Hypertensive shows flame‑shaped haemorrhages and cotton‑wool spots without microaneurysms; diabetic shows microaneurysms, hard exudates, and neovascularisation.

In a low‑resource clinic, what is the most cost‑effective strategy to prevent diabetic foot amputation? — Regular foot inspection, patient education, proper footwear, and early referral for any ulcer.
ai.title: Diabetic Complications
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Chronic hyperglycaemia causes micro‑ and macrovascular damage, leading to organ dysfunction. Recognising patterns, staging severity, and using limited investigations guide urgent and long‑term care in low‑resource settings.

b: Microvascular: retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy
Macrovascular: coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, peripheral arterial disease
sections.p: Complications are organ‑specific manifestations of chronic hyperglycaemia, confirmed by a history of diabetes (fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL or HbA1c ≥6.5 %) and evidence of end‑organ damage.

b: Retinopathy: mild non‑proliferative → proliferative → vision‑threatening
Neuropathy: symptoms → loss of ankle reflexes → ulceration
sections.p: Each complication has recognised stages; for example, diabetic retinopathy uses the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) scale, and nephropathy uses albumin‑creatinine ratio (ACR).

b: Poor glycaemic control (HbA1c >8 %)
Hypertension and dyslipidaemia
HIV infection or antiretroviral therapy
Chronic malaria or schistosomiasis causing anaemia and renal stress
Herbal nephrotoxins (e.g., Aristolochia)
sections.p: Sustained hyperglycaemia drives oxidative stress, advanced glycation end‑products, and sorbitol accumulation; co‑existing tropical infections and poor nutrition accelerate damage.

b: Retinopathy: blurred vision, floaters, sudden loss of vision
Nephropathy: peripheral oedema, hypertension, reduced urine output
Neuropathy: burning feet, loss of sensation, foot ulcer
Macrovascular disease: chest pain, claudication, stroke signs
sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic early; later they develop visual changes, swelling, pain, or ulceration depending on the organ involved.
When a test is unavailable, use clinical surrogates: visual acuity for retinopathy, blood pressure trends for nephropathy, and wound inspection for neuropathy.

t.b: average glucose over 3 months; >8 % indicates poor control and higher complication risk
screens peripheral neuropathy; loss of sensation predicts ulcer risk
detects peripheral arterial disease; <0.9 suggests significant disease
assesses renal function; eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² signals chronic kidney disease

b: Rapid visual loss → proliferative retinopathy with vitreous haemorrhage
Sudden rise in creatinine or oedema → acute kidney injury on chronic nephropathy
Deep foot ulcer with foul smell → osteomyelitis, possible sepsis
Chest pain with diaphoresis → acute coronary syndrome
sections.p: Unrecognised or untreated complications can rapidly become life‑threatening.

b: Intensive glycaemic control (metformin first line, insulin if needed) to slow progression
ACE inhibitor or ARB for nephropathy – reduces intraglomerular pressure
Statin for macrovascular risk – lowers LDL and stabilises plaques
Laser photocoagulation for proliferative retinopathy – prevents vision loss
Wound debridement, off‑loading, and antibiotics for foot ulcers – avoid amputation
Aspirin low dose for secondary cardiovascular prevention
sections.p: Control glucose, blood pressure, and lipids; treat the specific organ problem; provide supportive care.

b: HbA1c every 3 months; aim <7 % if feasible
Annual retinal exam; earlier if visual symptoms
Urine ACR every 6 months
Foot exam at each visit; educate on daily inspection
Blood pressure target <130/80 mmHg
Hypertensive retinopathy – flame‑shaped haemorrhages without microaneurysms
Chronic glomerulonephritis – active urinary sediment, low complement
Peripheral arterial disease from sickle cell – painful crises, not neuropathic pain
sections.p: Other causes of similar organ findings may be mistaken for diabetic complications.

b: Normal HbA1c in anaemic patients – may underestimate glucose exposure
Microalbuminuria can be transient after exercise or infection – repeat testing needed
Fundoscopy may miss early peripheral lesions – consider retinal photography if available
sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal in early disease or in low‑resource settings.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening leg swelling or shortness of breath
Severe foot pain with swelling or foul discharge
Chest pain radiating to arm or jaw
